topic: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings
scope_note: Practical guidance on structuring a single feedback comment so the receiver knows what to do differently. Does not cover formal performance review systems, disciplinary process, or written documentation requirements.

facts.statement: Feedback that names a feeling or a character judgement about the person rarely tells them what to repeat or stop doing
facts.caveat: This is a widely taught practitioner principle in feedback and coaching literature rather than a single settled experimental finding.

facts.statement: A behaviour is something that was directly seen or heard, such as a specific action or word choice, not an inference about intent or character
Naming a specific observed behaviour gives the other person something concrete they can recognise in themselves
facts.caveat: The mechanism is plausible and widely taught, though the sheet does not cite a controlled study showing the size of the effect.

facts.statement: Labels like unprofessional or careless describe a judgement, not a behaviour, so they leave the person guessing what action caused the label
Connecting a behaviour to its concrete impact on the work, team or outcome gives the person a reason to change it
facts.caveat: This is standard coaching practice; it is not claimed to be sufficient on its own without a clear next step.

facts.statement: A feedback comment that stops at an opinion, such as this needs to be better, does not tell the person what action to take next
Ending a feedback conversation with a clear, agreed next action makes it more likely the person's behaviour changes than ending with an opinion alone
facts.caveat: Widely taught in coaching and management practice; the sheet does not cite a controlled comparison of outcomes.

facts.statement: A next action is concrete when the person could start it within the same week without needing further clarification
Asking the other person for their view before fixing the next step increases the chance they agree with it and follow through
facts.caveat: This reflects common coaching guidance on collaborative goal setting rather than a single cited study.

facts.statement: A next step that the person helped shape is more likely to be one they actually attempt than one handed to them
facts.caveat: Plausible and widely taught, not backed here by a specific named study.

facts.statement: The three parts of a behaviour-based feedback comment are the specific behaviour observed, its impact, and the agreed next step
facts.caveat: This three-part structure is a common practitioner framework, presented here as a useful shape rather than a single validated model with a named origin.

facts.statement: Feedback can flow between peers or from a more junior person to a more senior one, not only from a manager down to a report
A tone that is warm or blunt in delivery does not by itself determine whether the receiver's behaviour changes afterward
facts.caveat: This reflects the practitioner view that clarity of the message matters more than delivery style; it is not a claim that tone never matters.

facts.statement: A vague comment can be rewritten by adding the missing behaviour, impact or next step without needing a new conversation

not_claimed: There is no fixed statistic for how much feedback changes behaviour or how often vague feedback fails
No specific named feedback model (such as a particular branded framework) is established fact; the behaviour, impact, next-step shape here is a generic practitioner pattern
Learning-styles or modality-matching claims are not supported and are not part of this topic
Harsh or blunt delivery is not claimed to be more effective than warm delivery, nor is warmth claimed to be sufficient on its own
Feedback is not claimed to work only when given by a manager to a direct report
